One of the best Indie games I've played in a long time. 

I normally think Indie games are hastily made, have a cookie cutter formula, and simply aren't fun or intresting, but this is one of the few among the masses that stands out. Its story is one of the best I've encountered in games for a very long time. The universe feels real and fleshed out. The characters are memorable and feel like actual humans. The art style is simple, yet so much better than the standard pixel-art graphics that most indie games have. I won't go over the gameplay nor the story much, as I feel as though it would spoil the charm of the game.

tl;dr - Buy Orwell, I hate indie games but this one is good.

Wow. Okay, completed two "episodes" meaning two days, and it's actually pretty gripping. You spend the whole time looking at an interface, examining articles and listening in on calls and the like to try to get information. This information is sometimes useless, sometimes incorrect, and sometimes marked as yellow, meaning that there's other information it conflicts with. I haven't really played too far, as I said I've only completed the second "episode" but it's pretty fun, and when I found that I had gotten the correct information to prevent a bombing, I breathed a sigh of relief.

This was such a nice game to play on the first playthrough. The feeling of mystery, analysing people and the buildup. I only wish decisions had more impact in the game. I will definitely be buying the second game at some point in the future! Hunting down the achievements was quite fun as well, so I highly recommend this game to anyone.

This is a game that you play for the story. It is not amazing, but slowly builds up a mystery and investigation that you are tasked to solve. The ideas at play in relation to the story are the best. It is hard to stop playing once the story ramps up half way through the game.  I had to finish it all on my second day playing. This is why I recommend it. 

I will say that the gameplay is not very engrossing. You make choices on what to tell the goverment. That is your choice and it does change the outcome of the story. What is not so great is that you are really just going between highlights the game tells you. Very linear in that way. Sometimes doing this gets wary. I wanted to be the investigator, but it does make sense that if something like this existed the AI would do most of the work and then ask a person to interpret it. So just be forewarned that the story may not be enough if gameplay is more your jam.

You check all this data and select which information you want to put on that person's police profile in order to solve a crime. You end up digging up a lot of information about everyone and trying to put all the pieces together.

Con: You can only choose from already highlighted information and new data will only unlock after you've shared other specific information.

So, the criticisms of this game have been well-aired by now, and I agree with many of them. Nevertheless, I found playing it pretty compelling, if just for the idea of putting myself in the shoes of an investigator given access to private surveillance data, and the fact that there is no way to keep your ethics pure here.

The game features you, an analyst for an Orwellian society where surveillance and spying on citizens has become the counter-measure of terrorism and crime. To fully understand the Orwell experience, I recommend you read 1984 by George Orwell or try and make pro-Trump comments on Facebook and be arrested by the thought-police.

Anyway, in here you read people's personal information, social network activity, blogs, personal messaging and calls. While you're at it, you will extract "datachunks", parts of highlighted data, to profile the people you're investigating, and to decide the best course of action. The catch in all of this is that your assistant, the one giving the orders to security teams, will only know the data your forward to him, and will act accordingly to that. Feeling like stopping that Tumblrina from getting wine? Forward the credit card info to your assistant, and you will prevent it. Feeling like killing a mother and leaving his child orphan? Go ahead!

Your choices have an impact on the nation.

Orwell is like a text adventure with an attitude.  This isn't a bad thing, just get ready to read most of what they game has to offer... even the simulated phone calls.
The game is short (I finished it in around 5 hours), the story is good but not stellar (the 3rd act seemed to take a few too many liberties with what the characters knew/understood in my mind).

There is some replayability to the game as you can make different choices with different outcomes, unfortunately you'll have to play through the whole game (as far as I was able to tell) instead of picking up from certain points of the story.  Since the game is so short, it's not all that bad.

This is not a game it's an experience. One that I would highly recommend to anyone, not just gamers. If you have thought about the consequences of surveillance, this experience is for you. I can't wait to get the other episodes.

A thought-provoking little gem and wonderful political commentary that I'm glad to have the pleasure of enjoying. I discovered a side of myself that I am not very proud of, as the game put me into the role of a borderline thought-police where it is not to my awareness that I was techicallly indulging in a malicious gratification that amounts to retribution and voyeurism. Between justice and ethics, the game forces you to take sides, to make choices that holds your own beliefs and philosophy accountable, and whether they are inherently free from ideological incoherence or not, no one will ever be innocent.

The writing is solid nearly all throughout the game, the setting is believeable and the characters are alive with personalities. Though near the ending, the writing occassionally felt artificial and unsensible, the thrill was thriving but it's ultimately cheapened by cliche predictable events and anticlimactic text log presentations, something performed by voice actors would've been much more dramatic and effective. Other than that, Orwell kept me on my toes from beginning to end, a thrillful experience regardless.
I love the concept, but there are space for improvements. Adding more interactions with the crime scene(CCTV, Evidence) would be a good start.
